SPD-HUBBLE-STScI-2004-33b.sy: *Description*:> Artist's Concept This animation shows the evolution of a planet-forming disc around a star. Initially, the young disc is bright and thick with dust, providing raw materials for building planets. In the first 10 million years or so, gaps appear within the disc as newborn planets coalesce out of the dust, clearing out a path. In time, this planetary "debris disc" thins out as gravitational interactions with numerous planets slowly sweep away the dust. Steady pressure from the starlight and solar winds also blows out the dust. a ring of comets called the Kuiper Belt. Leftover dust in the inner portion of the solar system is known as "zodiacal dust." Bright, young discs can be imaged directly by visible-light telescopes, such as NASA's Hubble Space Telescope. Older, fainter debris discs can be detected only by infrared telescopes like NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope, which sense the discs' dim heat. christians13thegodlessstate.sy: The last in a series of thirteen films in which Bamber Gascoigne traces the history of Christianity over nearly 2000 years, from its origin and early growth up to its continued survival today. In 1848, the year that Marx and Engels published the Communist Manifesto, an atheist revolution swept away the French monarchy. The first country to make atheism a policy of state was Russia, though Christianity in the USSR is far from dead. Lenin described religion as the opium of the masses, but it has been calculated that one out of every six Russians still goes to church. In Poland the strength of the Roman Catholic church is demonstrated by the large crowds that attend mass in the ideal socialist city of Nowa Huta. In Italy, the centre of Roman Catholicism, a town like San Gimignano is governed by a communist mayor, but there is no conflict between communism and Christianity on a local level, illustrating the unique ability of the faith to adapt and survive

xd-10124-india-technicolor-short-vwr.sy: Someone had the bright idea of sending Technicolor cameraman Jack Cardiff to India to film a series of travelogues. He came back with a series of images that have defined color cinematography to this day. More than eighty years later THE BEST EXOTIC MARIGOLD HOTEL still uses that brilliant white light and splashes of strong-chroma color, an effect like paintings on a whitewashed wall -- and completely different from the light he used for his British films. Cardiff was always the most painterly of the Technicolor cameramen and could achieve amazing effects -- once when Michael Powell said he wanted a slow fade in, Cardiff set the director behind the camera and breathed on the lens, fogging it: just the effect Powell had wanted.The modern audience may be more interested in the casual racism of the narrator -- referring to "mysteries that white men are forbidden" and so forth, but the joy of this film, as with Cardiff's other travel movies -- indeed, with every movie he worked on, starting as a child actor in the silent era and working until his death in his nineties, lay in the image. Enjoy it for that.
